title: New France
para1: New France. New France was the French colonial empire in North America, claimed for King Francis I when Jacques Cartier entered the Gulf of St. Lawrence in 1534. After an early colony near Quebec failed, the French fur trade with the First Nations took root, and Samuel de Champlain founded Port-Royal, the first French colony in North America, then in 1608 began the settlement of Quebec on a commanding site controlling the narrowing of the St. Lawrence. New France matters because its economy rested on the fur trade and on alliance with Indigenous nations rather than on mass settlement: the Company of New France held a monopoly of the trade in return for bringing settlers, missionaries aimed to convert the First Nations and excluded Huguenots, and vigorous young men slipped away from the seigneurial estates - where habitants farmed land granted by seigneurs in return for dues - to become coureurs de bois in the forests.
para2: Under royal rule the colony pushed far beyond the St. Lawrence: Louis Jolliet explored the Mississippi until he was sure it flowed into the Gulf of Mexico, and in 1699 Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville founded Louisiana, another part of New France. War with England shadowed the colony from the start - during King William's War a New England fleet under Sir William Phips seized Acadia, though Quebec defied his attack - and in 1700 and 1701 peace was made between the Iroquois and New France. The end came in the Seven Years' War: when peace was made by the Treaty of Paris in 1763, all New France east of the Mississippi, outside the environs of New Orleans, was ceded to Great Britain, and France kept only the two little islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon. French culture, however, survived the conquest - above all in Quebec, and in the Louisiana that passed through Spanish and French hands before ending up with the United States in 1804.

title: The American Revolution & Early Republic
titleline: The American Revolution & Early Republic - The History Web
para1: The American Revolution & Early Republic. The American Revolution was the insurrection fought between 1775 and 1783 through which thirteen of Great Britain's North American colonies threw off British rule and established the sovereign United States of America. It began on April 19, 1775, when British regulars skirmished with American provincials first at Lexington - where a British force of 700 faced 77 local minutemen - and then at Concord, after Britain's attempts to assert greater control over colonial affairs ended a long period of salutary neglect. On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence, written chiefly by Thomas Jefferson, announcing the separation of the thirteen colonies; the final vote for separation had actually come two days earlier, on July 2. This revolution matters because what began as a civil war within the British Empire became an international war - France joining the colonies in 1778 and Spain in 1779 - and turned colonial resistance into a new nation founded on an articulated ideal of self-government.
para2: The Continental Army commanded by George Washington, assisted by those crucial French and Spanish alliances, fought until the major fighting ended in 1781 and the peace treaty of 1783 recognized independence. The young republic first governed itself under the Articles of Confederation, but the Articles proved unworkable - the central government lacked essential powers - so delegates to the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia wrote the U.S. Constitution in 1787, the oldest written national constitution still in use. It created a federal system of balanced branches with checks and balances, and its first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, guaranteed fundamental rights and liberties to individuals. Yet the early republic also faced severe challenges - national debt, partisan polarization, and the unresolved moral contradiction of chattel slavery and indigenous displacement in a nation dedicated to liberty.
source3label: Smarthistory: The American Revolution and Early Republic

title: The Colonial Caribbean (Spanish, French, British, Dutch)
titleline: The Colonial Caribbean (Spanish, French, British, Dutch) - The History Web
para1: The Colonial Caribbean. The colonial Caribbean - the Spanish Main and the West Indian islands - was the first American world conquered by Europe. Spain settled Puerto Rico and then Cuba in 1511, introduced cattle, horses, and mules, and created plantations growing sugar cane, just as the Portuguese had done on Atlantic islands like Madeira; native peoples were ruthlessly robbed, butchered, or enslaved, and perhaps two million African slaves were shipped to the Spanish Main in the 16th and 17th centuries. The riches were guarded jealously - Havana, from 1610, boasted the largest shipyard in the Americas - but the other empires muscled in: the English planted St. Kitts in 1623, Barbados in 1624, and Nevis, Antigua, and Montserrat by 1632, the French took Martinique and Guadeloupe in 1635, and from 1599 Dutch ships loaded salt at Araya.
para2: The seventeenth century became the great age of the buccaneers: when the English seized Jamaica with its wonderful natural harbours in 1655, the entire Spanish Main lay open to attack, and privateers sponsored by the colonial authorities struck its ports - Henry Morgan sacked Panama in 1671 and ransomed Portobelo in 1680, pirates raided Veracruz in 1683 and made off with the loot meant for a treasure fleet, and a French naval and pirate force captured Cartagena in 1697, the last major buccaneer raid. The islands produced sugar, tobacco, coffee, and cotton through the horrific business of slavery, and they matter because their plantations bound Europe, Africa, and the Americas into a single Atlantic economy. French rule in Saint-Domingue ended in 1804 with the only successful slave revolt in history, and through the 1820s the Latin American nations declared independence from Spain, with rebel forces besieging and taking even Cartagena in 1815 and 1821.

title: The Confederation of Canada
titleline: The Confederation of Canada - The History Web
para1: The Confederation of Canada. The Confederation of Canada was the process by which the three British North American colonies of the mid-19th century - the Province of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick - united to form the Dominion of Canada. Fueled by the fear of possible American aggression and by economic ambition, politicians and the public debated merging the colonies into one self-governing confederation; with British support, representatives negotiated the terms of their union at conferences in Charlottetown and Quebec, where Sir John A. Macdonald and Cartier joined with their chief opponent George Brown to further the scheme. The result was the British North America Act, passed in 1867 and put into effect on July 1 - now celebrated as Canada Day - creating a new country of four provinces: Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, with the former Province of Canada split into Ontario and Quebec. This union matters because it created the stable federal framework from which a transcontinental nation would grow.
para2: Confederation did not yet mean independence: the new law established Canada as a semi-independent 'Dominion' of the British Empire, without full autonomy, and the journey toward full independence continued for decades - after the First World War, Canada joined the other dominions in seeking formal recognition of its independence, reaching a milestone in 1931. Macdonald, the Dominion's first prime minister (1867-73, 1878-91), dominated the early decades: forced to resign in 1873 by the Pacific Scandal - in which his government was accused of taking bribes over the Pacific railway contract - he returned five years later and applied his policy of trade protectionism swiftly and thoroughly. Over the decades that followed, Canada expanded across the continent, absorbing vast northern and western territories and additional provinces, and transformed itself from a cluster of colonies into a modern transcontinental nation.

title: The Haitian Revolution
titleline: The Haitian Revolution - The History Web
para1: The Haitian Revolution. The Haitian Revolution was the only successful slave revolt in history: an anti-slavery and anti-colonial insurrection that convulsed the French colony of Saint-Domingue from 1791 to 1804 and led directly to the founding of an independent state. On the eve of the uprising the colony held some 556,000 people - roughly half a million enslaved Africans alongside 32,000 European colonists and 24,000 affranchis, free people of color - and the enslaved majority endured backbreaking workdays on the sugar plantations, often dying from injuries and exhaustion. When revolution broke out in France, the colonists' rival factions fought over the Declaration of the Rights of Man, and in October 1790 the affranchi Vincent Oge led an unsuccessful revolt; the following year the enslaved themselves rose, and the former slave Toussaint Louverture became their great leader. This revolution matters because it shattered the foundations of Atlantic slavery and terrified slaveholding regimes across the Western Hemisphere.
para2: Toussaint proved a master strategist: first fighting alongside Spain, he abandoned his Spanish allies when the French Republic abolished slavery in 1794, rose to commander-in-chief of the island by 1797, defeated Spanish and British forces, conquered Santo Domingo in 1801, and had himself named governor-general for life. Napoleon answered by sending his brother-in-law, General Charles Leclerc, with an experienced army to restore French rule; Toussaint struggled for months, agreed to an armistice in May 1802, and was then seized and exiled to France. The fighting continued under Jean-Jacques Dessalines and Henry Christophe, whose forces prevailed over the French, and in 1804 Dessalines declared Haiti independent, giving the territory its new name. The price of survival was steep: France withheld recognition until 1825, and then only in exchange for an indemnity of 100 million francs that - together with diplomatic isolation - burdened the young republic's development for generations.
source2label: Humanities LibreTexts: 4.4: Sugar and the Haitian Revolution
source3label: PBS: Africans in America/Part 3/The Haitian Revolution

title: The Mexican Empire & First Republic
titleline: The Mexican Empire & First Republic - The History Web
para1: The Mexican Empire and First Republic. The Mexican Empire was the brief monarchy that spanned the transition from colony to independent republic. When Agustin de Iturbide's Army of the Three Guarantees secured independence in 1821, independence from the former mother country had been the only glue binding republicans and monarchists together; in 1822 Iturbide crowned himself Emperor Agustin I, and towns across Mexico swore recognition and obedience to 'Agustin Primero' on December 8, 1822 - the celebrated Poblano prints record those oaths, printed on sheets of gold, silver, and bronze alloy. The experiment collapsed within months: revolts found their pretext, General Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna among the rebel leaders, and Agustin was forced to reconvene congress and abdicate; in 1824 he returned from European exile, but was arrested and shot.
para2: The constitution of 1824 made Mexico a federal republic of nineteen states, four territories, and the Mexico City federal district, and Guadalupe Victoria, a leader of the independence movement, was elected its first president. But the pendulum of power swung between Centralists, who favored a strong national army and Roman Catholicism as the exclusive religion, and Federalists, who favored limited central government and nearly autonomous states - a struggle dominated for a third of a century by the charismatic Santa Anna. When Santa Anna's new constitution of 1836 eliminated all vestiges of states' rights, Texas revolted; Santa Anna trapped and eliminated the Alamo garrison, but was defeated and captured by Texas forces in April 1836. The United States annexed the Republic of Texas in 1845, Mexican and U.S. patrols clashed in April 1846, and the Mexican-American War that followed ended in 1848 with Mexico giving up its claims to Texas and ceding the territories of today's California, Utah, Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona, and beyond - the humiliating dismemberment of almost half the national territory.

title: The Mexican War of Independence
titleline: The Mexican War of Independence - The History Web
para1: The Mexican War of Independence. The Mexican War of Independence was an armed conflict that lasted from 1810 to 1821, ending three centuries of Spanish rule. It began with the Grito de Dolores - the 'Cry of Dolores' - uttered on September 16, 1810 by Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, the parish priest of Dolores, a highly educated creole who had read the Enlightenment writers. Calling upon peasants and unemployed miners to rise against the viceroyalty's government, Hidalgo demanded not only liberation from Spain but the abolition of slavery and tribute, the redistribution of wealth, and the return of land to the Indigenous people, and he marched under a banner of the Virgin of Guadalupe, proclaimed the rebellion's guardian and protector. His movement gathered a huge popular mob-army, but after much reckless pillage and bloodshed it was checked; Hidalgo was captured and executed on July 30, 1811. His 'cry' became the cry of independence, commemorated each year on the night of September 16.
para2: Jose Maria Morelos, another revolutionary priest and an organizer of artisans and peasants, took up the campaign with clear sociopolitical objectives: an end to slavery and the casta system, the abolition of Indigenous tribute, and independence from Spain. In his Sentiments of the Nation, composed to guide the congress he had charged with producing a constitution, Morelos listed twenty-three points he believed would create a strong nation capable of protecting all its people; but after Morelos's death his follower, the casta Vicente Guerrero, continued guerrilla operations against Spanish authorities for several more years, until Agustin de Iturbide - a royalist creole officer who had distinguished himself in the campaigns against Hidalgo and Morelos - changed sides. In 1821 Iturbide formed an agreement with the rebel leader Vicente Guerrero and issued the Plan of Iguala, built on the Three Guarantees of independence, religion, and equality: Mexico would be independent of Spain, Roman Catholicism the official religion, and criollos and peninsulares equal in rights. Their Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City in triumph, and on August 24, 1821, with the signing of the Treaty of Cordoba, Spain finally recognized the independence of Mexico.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Mexican War of Independence (Disambiguation)

title: The Thirteen Colonies & British America
titleline: The Thirteen Colonies & British America - The History Web
para1: The Thirteen Colonies & British America. The Thirteen Colonies were the British settlements planted along the Atlantic coast of North America between 1607 and 1732. It began when the Virginia Company established Jamestown in 1607 - a colony that nearly perished in the 'Starving Time' of 1609-10, when as many as 350 of the estimated 500 colonists died - and was saved when John Rolfe's tobacco seed from Bermuda took to the fertile Chesapeake soil, Virginia soon outstripping the West Indies as the main exporter of tobacco to Europe. In 1620 the Mayflower brought 102 Puritan separatists, the 'Pilgrims', to Massachusetts, and in 1630 John Winthrop led the Puritan 'Great Migration' to New England; the chain of colonies was completed in 1732, when Georgia was established as a buffer zone between the Carolinas and the hostile Spanish. These colonies matter because they developed robust traditions of local self-governance and representative assemblies, elected by propertied citizens, which the colonists prized as the shield of their rights.
para2: The colonies fell into three administrative categories - charter, royal, and proprietary - Virginia becoming the first royal colony when its company went bankrupt in 1624; New England was founded primarily by Puritans seeking religious freedom, while the Chesapeake drew poor young fortune-seekers seduced by the promise of the lucrative tobacco trade. From the earliest days of Jamestown the English also waged war with the Native Americans upon whose lands they were encroaching. Operating under British imperial mercantilism, the colonies long enjoyed considerable freedom from London, but the expensive French and Indian War changed the imperial mood: taxes such as the Sugar Act (1764) and the Stamp Act (1765), aimed at raising revenue from the colonies, outraged the colonists and catalyzed a resistance that forged a shared political identity among the thirteen colonies - and led directly to the American Revolutionary War.
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: Chapter 3: British North America

title: The Viceroyalty of New Spain
titleline: The Viceroyalty of New Spain - The History Web
para1: The Viceroyalty of New Spain. The Viceroyalty of New Spain was the first of the four viceroyalties that Spain created to govern its conquered lands in the New World. Established in 1535, fourteen years after the fall of Tenochtitlan, it initially embraced all Spanish-controlled land north of the Isthmus of Panama, and later grew to take in upper and lower California, the future southwestern United States, the Gulf coast eastward to Florida, Spain's Caribbean possessions, and from 1565 even the newly conquered Philippines. Administered from Mexico City for three centuries, this administration matters deeply because it was the first great template of Spanish rule in the Americas, integrating the hemisphere into global commerce through an economy based almost entirely on mining and ranching, while its viceroys sponsored the conversion of the Native population to Christianity and built an array of educational institutions.
para2: The viceroy, appointed by the Spanish Crown, was technically the supreme authority, yet in practice the considerable independence of governors and royal audiencias in the subordinate regions confined his real power largely to central and southern Mexico. The first viceroy, Antonio de Mendoza, who ruled from 1535 to 1549, dispatched Francisco Coronado on his expedition northward while ameliorating some of the worst abuses of the conquistadores and supporting the church's work with the Native population. That mission came at a terrible cost: during the first hundred years of Spanish rule, the Indigenous population of New Spain collapsed from an estimated 25 million to 1 million through maltreatment, disease, and the disruption of their cultures, while a casta hierarchy - famously catalogued in the viceroyalty's paintings - stratified society by ancestry. After a period of decline in the late seventeenth century, distinguished viceroys such as Bucareli and Revillagigedo revived the administration and pushed settlement overland into California to counter Russian and British interest; the viceroyalty weathered the early independence risings of Hidalgo and Morelos, only to succumb to Agustin de Iturbide's coalition in 1821.

title: The Kingdom and Empire of Haiti
titleline: The Kingdom and Empire of Haiti - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom and Empire of Haiti. The Kingdom and Empire of Haiti (1804-1820) arose from the world's only successful slave revolution. When Haiti declared independence in 1804, its leaders faced the task of building a state from a shattered plantation society. Jean-Jacques Dessalines, the hero of the war, proclaimed himself emperor in 1804, but after his assassination in 1806 the country split in two: a republic in the south under Alexandre Petion, and in the north the kingdom of Henri Christophe, a former slave who had become one of the revolution's greatest generals and who was crowned King Henry I in 1811.
para2: Christophe's kingdom was an astonishing experiment in Black statehood. The king created a Haitian nobility with dukes and barons, a court, an army, and a code of laws, and he drove his people to rebuild the economy and raise monuments to their freedom. The greatest of these was the Citadelle Laferriere, the vast fortress on the peak above Cap-Haitien, built to defy any French attempt to reconquer the island, and below it the palace of Sans-Souci, the Versailles of the Caribbean. Yet Christophe's rule was severe: his system of forced plantation labor kept the estates producing but weighed heavily on the people.
para3: The kingdom did not outlive its founder. In 1820, stricken by paralysis and facing revolt, Christophe shot himself in his palace; his heir was soon murdered, and the north was absorbed into the southern republic of Jean-Pierre Boyer, which reunited Haiti and then ruled the whole island of Hispaniola for two decades. Dessalines' empire and Christophe's kingdom alike passed into legend.
para4: Their meaning endures. The Black kingdom and empire of Haiti proved that the revolution was no accident and that a state founded by freed slaves could govern itself and build monuments to rival those of Europe. The Citadelle, now a UNESCO World Heritage site, remains the supreme symbol of Haitian independence.
source2label: Library of Congress Country Studies: Christophe's Kingdom and Petion's Republic
source3label: The Conversation: Inside the Kingdom of Haiti

title: The Mexican-American War
titleline: The Mexican-American War - The History Web
para1: The Mexican-American War. The Mexican-American War (1846-1848) redrew the map of North America. Its roots lay in Texas, which had broken from Mexico in 1836 and was annexed by the United States in 1845. Mexico had never accepted Texan independence, and the two nations disputed the border: Mexico claimed the Nueces River, the United States the Rio Grande. When American troops under Zachary Taylor marched into the disputed land in 1846 and blood was shed, President James K. Polk, an ardent expansionist, secured a declaration of war.
para2: The war was fought on three fronts. Taylor's army won battles at Monterrey and Buena Vista in northern Mexico; an American column under Stephen Kearny seized New Mexico and California, where settlers had already proclaimed the Bear Flag Republic; and in the decisive campaign, General Winfield Scott landed at Veracruz in the first great amphibious operation of the American army and marched on Mexico City, storming the fortress of Chapultepec, where the young cadets remembered as the Ninos Heroes died in its defense. Mexico City fell in September 1847.
para3: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed in February 1848, ended the war on terms that transformed the continent. Mexico recognized the loss of Texas and ceded to the United States the vast territory of California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, and parts of Colorado, Wyoming, and New Mexico, half of its national territory, in return for fifteen million dollars. Some hundred thousand Mexicans suddenly found themselves citizens of the United States.
para4: The war made the United States a continental power but deepened the quarrel over slavery that would soon tear it apart: the question of slavery in the new lands led within a dozen years to civil war. In Mexico the defeat left a lasting wound and a long memory, and the war remains one of the most consequential, and most contested, in the history of both nations.

title: The Antebellum South
titleline: The Antebellum South - The History Web
para1: The Antebellum South. The Antebellum South (1820-1861) was the slaveholding society of the American South in the decades before the Civil War, an era when cotton was king. The invention of the cotton gin and the hunger of the world's textile mills made upland cotton fantastically profitable, and plantation slavery spread across the Deep South, from South Carolina and Georgia to Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas. By 1860 the region held some four million enslaved African Americans, and its cotton supplied most of the world's mills.
para2: Slavery was the foundation of everything. Enslaved people worked the fields in gangs under overseers, cleared new lands, and labored in houses, workshops, and cities; they were bought and sold, their families broken by sale, and their labor built the wealth of the planter class and much of the nation. The enslaved resisted in countless ways, through work slowdowns, escape, and the preservation of family, faith, and culture, and in rare open revolts such as Nat Turner's rising of 1831, after which the southern states tightened their slave codes still further.
para3: White southern society was dominated by the planter elite, though most white families owned no slaves. Planters ruled the statehouses and much of the national government, celebrated a code of honor and paternalism, and increasingly defended slavery not as a necessary evil but as a positive good. As the North industrialized and antislavery feeling grew, the sections clashed repeatedly over the spread of slavery into the western territories.
para4: The conflict could not be contained. The election of Abraham Lincoln in 1860, on a platform opposing the extension of slavery, drove the cotton states to secede, and in 1861 the country descended into civil war. Defeat destroyed slavery and the world the planters had made, but the legacy of the antebellum South, in race, wealth, and memory, has shaped America ever since.

title: The Plains Indian Wars
titleline: The Plains Indian Wars - The History Web
para1: The Plains Indian Wars. The Plains Indian Wars (1854-1890) were the long struggle of the Native peoples of the Great Plains against the expansion of the United States. The horse and the buffalo had made the Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, and Kiowa some of the finest light cavalry in the world, and for two centuries they ruled the plains. But after the Civil War, American settlers, miners, and railroads poured west, treaties were made and broken, and the buffalo herds were systematically destroyed, dooming the way of life they supported.
para2: The wars flared for a generation. On the northern plains, Red Cloud's warriors forced the United States in 1868 to abandon the Bozeman Trail, the only war in which the government accepted an Indian nation's terms. In 1876, when the army moved against the Lakota and Cheyenne over the Black Hills, the allied warriors led by Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse annihilated George Custer's command at the Little Bighorn. But the victory could not be sustained: the army pursued the bands without rest, Crazy Horse was killed in 1877, and Sitting Bull surrendered in 1881. In the south, the Comanche and their allies fought until the Red River War of 1874-75 drove them onto the reservations.
para3: The end came at Wounded Knee. In 1890, as the Lakota turned in despair to the Ghost Dance religion, the army moved to disarm them, and at Wounded Knee Creek soldiers killed some two hundred and fifty Lakota, many of them women and children. It was the last armed confrontation of the Plains wars.
para4: The wars decided the fate of a continent. The Plains nations were confined to reservations on poor land, their children sent to boarding schools meant to erase their cultures, their treaty lands whittled away. Yet the Lakota, Cheyenne, and Comanche nations survive, and the memory of Red Cloud, Sitting Bull, and Crazy Horse remains a touchstone of resistance and identity for Native America.

title: Rupert's Land and the Hudson's Bay Company
titleline: Rupert's Land and the Hudson's Bay Company - The History Web
para1: Rupert's Land and the Hudson's Bay Company. Rupert's Land (1670-1870) was the vast territory of northern North America granted by King Charles II to the Hudson's Bay Company, the oldest chartered company in Canadian history. In 1670 the king gave his cousin Prince Rupert and his fellow adventurers a monopoly over all the lands draining into Hudson Bay, nearly four million square kilometers, almost half of modern Canada. From a string of trading posts on the bay, beginning with York Factory, the Company drew the furs of a continent.
para2: The Company's empire rested on partnership with the First Nations. Cree, Assiniboine, and other Indigenous hunters and traders brought beaver and other furs to the bay posts or to company traders inland, exchanging them for guns, cloth, metal tools, and brandy, and the fur trade tied the peoples of the north into the commerce of Europe. Competition with French traders from Montreal, and later with the North West Company, drove the HBC inland up the great rivers, until in 1821 the two rivals merged under the Hudson's Bay name.
para3: The trade transformed the region. New mixed-descent peoples, the Metis of the Red River, emerged as buffalo hunters, traders, and farmers, while the company ruled its territory like a government, with courts, forts, and a governor. But the settlement of the prairies and the pressure of Canada could not be resisted forever, and in 1870 the Company surrendered Rupert's Land to the new Dominion of Canada, keeping its posts and rich land grants.
para4: The legacy of Rupert's Land is Canada itself: the fur trade drew the map of the northern half of the continent, its routes became the paths of settlement, and its conflicts live on in the history of the First Nations and the Metis, who rose at Red River to defend their land and rights. The Hudson's Bay Company still trades today, the oldest company in North America.
source3label: Rupertsland Institute: What is Rupert's Land

title: The Cuban Wars of Independence
titleline: The Cuban Wars of Independence - The History Web
para1: The Cuban Wars of Independence. The Cuban Wars of Independence (1868-1898) were the thirty-year struggle that ended four centuries of Spanish rule in Cuba. The island, Spain's richest remaining colony, was a world of sugar plantations worked by hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans, and its Creole landowners chafed under Spanish rule and taxation. In 1868 the planter Carlos Manuel de Cespedes freed his slaves and proclaimed the Grito de Yara, launching the Ten Years' War, the first great war of Cuban independence.
para2: The first war devastated the east of the island without winning freedom. Under generals such as Maximo Gomez and the Black hero Antonio Maceo, the rebels fought Spain to a standstill, but divisions and exhaustion brought an uneasy peace in 1878. A second rising, the Little War of 1879-80, also failed, though slavery itself was finally abolished in 1886. Yet the cause lived on, above all in the writings of Jose Marti, the poet and organizer who built the Cuban Revolutionary Party among the exiles and workers of the diaspora.
para3: In 1895 Marti and Gomez launched the final war. Marti was killed in one of its first battles, but the war swept west across the island: Gomez and Maceo led the invasion army from east to west, and Spain, under General Weyler, answered with the brutal policy of reconcentration, herding the rural population into camps where tens of thousands died. By 1898 Spain could neither win nor withdraw, and the explosion of the American battleship Maine in Havana harbor brought the United States into the war.
para4: The Spanish-American War ended in months, and Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines. Cuba became independent in name but an American protectorate in fact, occupied and bound by the Platt Amendment. Marti's dream of a free and sovereign Cuba, deferred in 1898, remained the standard by which Cubans judged the century that followed.

title: The Federal Republic of Central America
titleline: The Federal Republic of Central America - The History Web
para1: The Federal Republic of Central America was an ambitious attempt to keep the five former Spanish provinces of Central America united after independence, and its failure shaped the region's political map to this day. When Mexico's Agustín de Iturbide abdicated in 1823, the Central American provinces of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica, which had been briefly annexed to his empire, declared their independence and formed a federation modeled on the United States. A constituent assembly in Guatemala City drafted a constitution in 1824, creating a federal republic with an elected president, a congress, and a senate.
para2: The federation's first and most celebrated leader was Francisco Morazán, a Honduran lawyer and general who became the republic's great champion. Morazán led the Liberal faction, which favored free trade, secular education, and limits on the power of the Catholic Church. The Liberals faced fierce opposition from Conservatives, who defended the church's privileges and the interests of the old colonial elite centered in Guatemala City. Morazán won the civil war of 1826-1829, captured the capital, and pushed through liberal reforms, moving the federal capital to San Salvador.
para3: The republic was chronically weak, however. The federal government lacked money, a real army, and the loyalty of the state governments, which frequently defied it. Geography worked against unity too: rugged mountains and terrible roads made the states feel like separate worlds. In 1837 a massive cholera epidemic swept Guatemala, and Conservative agitators convinced terrified peasants that Liberal officials had poisoned the wells. The resulting uprising, led by the charismatic Rafael Carrera, destroyed Liberal power in Guatemala, and the federation began to disintegrate as Nicaragua, Honduras, and Costa Rica seceded in 1838-1839.
para4: Morazán fought on desperately to restore the union, even returning from exile in 1842 to seize power in Costa Rica, but he was overthrown and executed by firing squad in San José that same year. The dream of Central American unity never entirely died: several attempts at reunion followed in the nineteenth century, and the five nations still share the five-volcano motif on their flags and a common court and parliament today. Morazán himself is honored as a national hero in Honduras and El Salvador, and Honduras's Morazán department bears his name.

title: William Walker and the Filibusters
titleline: William Walker and the Filibusters - The History Web
para1: In the 1850s, bands of armed American adventurers called filibusters launched private invasions of Latin American countries, hoping to seize territory and create new slaveholding states. The word came from the Spanish filibustero, meaning freebooter or pirate, and it captured exactly what these expeditions were: illegal private wars of conquest. The filibuster movement grew out of the spirit of Manifest Destiny and the expansionist fervor that had recently won the United States half of Mexico's territory. Southern slaveholders especially looked south for new lands where slavery could expand, since the balance of free and slave states was becoming the nation's great political crisis.
para2: The most famous filibuster was William Walker, a slight, soft-spoken Tennessean who had trained as a doctor and lawyer before turning to conquest. Walker first invaded Mexico's Baja California in 1853, proclaiming the Republic of Sonora before his ragged band was driven back across the border. Acquitted of violating neutrality laws by a sympathetic California jury, Walker turned his attention to Nicaragua, which was then torn by civil war between its Liberal and Conservative parties. In 1855, hired by the Liberals, Walker landed with fewer than sixty men, seized the Conservative stronghold of Granada, and within months made himself the effective ruler of the country.
para3: Walker's Nicaraguan regime won diplomatic recognition from the United States in 1856, but his next moves destroyed him. He revoked the charter of Cornelius Vanderbilt's Accessory Transit Company, which controlled the vital steamer route across Nicaragua between the Atlantic and Pacific, and the enraged Vanderbilt bankrolled a coalition against him. Walker also reinstated slavery, hoping to win Southern support, which alienated Nicaraguans. In 1856-1857 the combined armies of the Central American republics, backed by Vanderbilt's agents, besieged Walker's forces at Rivas, where disease and hunger did most of the killing. Walker surrendered to the U.S. Navy in May 1857.
para4: Walker returned to Central America twice more. After a failed 1858 landing, he made his last attempt in 1860, landing on the coast of Honduras to support English-speaking settlers. Captured by the British Navy and handed over to Honduran authorities, he was executed by firing squad at Trujillo on September 12, 1860. The filibuster era left a deep mark on Central American memory, where the war against Walker is remembered as a war of national liberation, and Costa Rica still celebrates the hero Juan Santamaría, who died setting fire to a filibuster stronghold at the Battle of Rivas.
